title: ICE Seeks $470,000 Fine Against Indian-Origin Lawyer Over Fake Asylum Filings
excerpt: New York attorney Suraj Raj Singh allegedly filed 118 fraudulent documents in 54 cases — the second enforcement action in two months targeting lawyers who represent Indian asylum seekers.
body:
• ICE is seeking a $470,584 civil fine against New York attorney Suraj Raj Singh for allegedly filing 118 fraudulent documents across 54 immigration cases.
  • Singh's practice primarily represents Indian nationals seeking asylum, and the government alleges his clients' declarations contained "identical or nearly identical" persecution narratives.
  • The action follows a similar $255,000 fine against attorney Vinod Doddamani last month for filing 64 fraudulent documents in 32 cases — also involving Indian asylum seekers.
  • The crackdown marks an escalation in the Trump administration's use of financial penalties against immigration lawyers, a tool authorized under federal law in May.

A Pattern of Identical Claims

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced Thursday it is seeking more than $470,000 in civil fines against Suraj Raj Singh, a New York-based immigration attorney whose nationwide practice primarily serves Indian nationals seeking asylum. The agency alleges Singh filed 118 fraudulent documents across 54 cases, each containing "identical or nearly identical" narratives describing persecution.

https://x.com/OwenGregorian/status/2082813501278503340

According to DHS, the declarations Singh prepared for his clients shared "the same or nearly the same factual narrative and supporting details regarding the claimed persecution" — a pattern that ICE says demonstrates systematic fraud rather than legitimate case preparation.

Singh, who describes his practice on LinkedIn as handling "all kinds of immigration and corporation matters," did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.

Second Indian-Origin Lawyer Targeted

The action against Singh is the second enforcement case in as many months targeting an immigration attorney who primarily represents Indian nationals. In June, ICE announced it would seek a $255,232 fine against attorney Vinod Doddamani for allegedly filing 64 fraudulent documents in 32 immigration cases.

Like Singh, Doddamani operates a nationwide practice and mostly represents Indian asylum seekers. ICE alleged his declarations followed the same template pattern — near-identical persecution narratives submitted on behalf of different clients. Doddamani also did not respond to a request for comment.

"Fraudulent asylum claims threaten the safety of the American people, undermine our immigration system, and delay the removal of dangerous criminal illegal aliens."

— James Percival, DHS General Counsel

A New Enforcement Tool

The fines reflect the Trump administration's expanding use of a tool authorized in May, when the Department of Homeland Security directed ICE to pursue civil penalties against immigration attorneys for alleged document fraud. Under federal law, individuals accused of document fraud in an immigration context are entitled to a hearing before an administrative law judge and can seek judicial review.

The Notice of Intent to Fine is a proposed civil enforcement action, meaning Singh will have an opportunity to respond before any penalty is finalized. However, immigration attorneys say the fines — which represent the maximum permissible amounts — are designed as much to deter as to punish.

Impact on Indian Asylum Seekers

The crackdown carries significant implications for the growing number of Indian nationals seeking asylum in the United States. Indian asylum applications have surged in recent years, driven by a combination of religious persecution claims, political dissent, and economic migration. The number of Indians apprehended at the U.S.-Mexico border rose sharply in 2024 and 2025.

Immigration advocates have expressed concern that high-profile fraud cases could be used to cast doubt on legitimate asylum claims from Indian nationals, many of whom face genuine threats. At the same time, attorneys practicing in the field say fraudulent filings by a small number of practitioners damage the credibility of all Indian asylum cases.

What's Next

Both cases are in their preliminary stages, and neither Singh nor Doddamani has been criminally charged. The fines are civil penalties, not criminal sanctions. However, the DHS has signaled that more enforcement actions are forthcoming, with General Counsel Percival warning that the administration will "hold attorneys like this accountable."

For Indian immigrants navigating the asylum system, the cases underscore the importance of thorough, individualized legal representation — and the risks of cut-rate attorneys who prioritize volume over substance.
